title: How Did LayerZero Build The Connective Tissue Of The Multi-Chain World?
gist: ARK argues cross-chain messaging has become one of crypto's largest primitives — $580B of cross-chain value transferred year-to-date, on track for $1T+ — and that LayerZero won it by moving verified messages rather than custodying assets, taking 44% of H1 2026 cross-chain volume vs 41% for Circle's CCTP, with OFT holding 80-90% share of cross-chain token standards. The deeper thesis: the capital premium for launching new chains has collapsed, fragmentation is reversing into consolidation, and LayerZero's five years of integrating 170+ chains is the springboard for a new L1 called Zero, detailed in Part 2. ARK discloses it is an investor in LayerZero Labs and the ZRO token.

themes.theme: Cross-Chain As A Top-3 Crypto Primitive

insights.claim: Cross-chain value transfers across all bridging and messaging mechanisms totaled $580 billion year-to-date as of mid-2026 and are on track to clear $1+ trillion for the year, roughly 4x the size of all prediction markets and more than half of all DEX spot volume.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Sizes the interoperability market against better-covered categories: if cross-chain is already a top-3 crypto primitive by volume, the infrastructure capturing it is undermonetized relative to DEX and perps venues that get most of the attention.
insights.quote: cross-chain value transfers have totaled $580 billion and are on track to clear $1+ trillion for the year
insights.locator: Highlighting the structural problem is the scale

insights.claim: By volume, cross-chain transfers now rank among the largest primitives in all of crypto, exceeded only by perpetual futures and spot trading.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Ranking interoperability behind only perps and spot argues for treating messaging protocols as core financial infrastructure rather than a niche middleware bet.
insights.locator: By volume, cross-chain transfers now rank

insights.claim: Blockchains are hermetically sealed programmable ledgers with no native awareness of each other — Ethereum does not know what happens on Solana — so every asset confined to one chain has an addressable market capped by that ecosystem's participants and is functionally less useful.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Frames omnichain issuance as an addressable-market expansion, not a convenience feature — the valuation lens for tokens and tokenized assets that adopt unified-supply standards.
insights.quote: Ethereum does not know what is happening on Solana. Solana does not know what is happening on Arbitrum.
insights.locator: Framing And Thesis

insights.claim: Because tokens could not interact with contracts on other chains, applications migrated toward liquidity instead — Aave and Uniswap have deployed the same code across dozens of chains while activity still concentrates in a few, a duplication cost imposed purely by fragmentation.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Multi-chain deployment is overhead, not growth: if messaging removes the need for app replication, engineering budgets and incentive spend at major DeFi protocols should compress.
insights.locator: Because tokens could not interact with contracts

insights.claim: Three distinct forces drove blockchain fragmentation — technical necessity (Ethereum's EVM was constantly at capacity), capital incentives (investors paid multiples for teams launching their own chains), and architectural specialization (a derivatives DEX cannot share a fee market with NFT mints or meme coin launches) — and only by separating them can a solution be designed.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A usable decomposition for handicapping consolidation: two of the three forces are engineering problems that a better base layer can absorb, while the third is a market-pricing phenomenon that has already reversed.
insights.locator: The Fragmentation Problem

insights.claim: Ethereum's response to hitting throughput and bandwidth limits was not to scale the base layer but to encourage more chains via the rollup-centric roadmap, which ARK treats as the origin of the fragmentation problem rather than its solution.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: An implicit critique of the L2 thesis: if rollups were a workaround for an unscaled base layer, high-throughput monolithic L1s take share as the workaround becomes unnecessary.
insights.quote: Ethereum's answer was not to scale the base layer but to "launch more chains,"
insights.locator: Technical Necessity.

insights.claim: Chain proliferation was fundamentally a monetization phenomenon — new L1s and L2s with tokens were valued at multiples of the same application deployed on someone else's chain, so teams launched chains because the market paid them to.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Explains why chain counts were a function of token-market pricing, meaning the count should fall as that premium disappears — a leading indicator for L2/app-chain token supply.
insights.quote: The monetization model rewarded chain proliferation, so chains proliferated.
insights.locator: Capital Incentives.

insights.claim: Screening every L1, L2 and app-chain for over $20 million in TVL or over $50 million in market cap leaves roughly 150 chains, with L1 launches dominating through 2020, L2s such as Arbitrum and Optimism arriving after Ethereum formalized the rollup roadmap, and app-chains like Hyperliquid and dYdX rising as a share of launches into 2023-2024.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A concrete denominator for the fragmentation trade — ~150 economically relevant chains defines both the integration surface for interop protocols and the pool of tokens exposed to consolidation.
insights.locator: we have compiled most Layer 1, Layer 2, and app-chains

insights.claim: The four largest chains each won a distinct function — Bitcoin for settlement, Ethereum for programmability, Solana for throughput, Hyperliquid for perpetuals — while a nontrivial amount of capital still sits in a long tail of chains optimizing for different goals despite power-law dynamics.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A function-based map of the majors, and an argument that long-tail chains retain enough capital to keep interoperability demand alive even under winner-take-most dynamics.
insights.locator: The largest four are Bitcoin for settlement

insights.claim: Bridges holding custody of large asset pools became the highest-value attack surfaces in crypto, with Ronin losing $625 million to compromised validator keys, Wormhole $325 million to a signature verification bug, and Multichain over $130 million when operator keys were compromised and its CEO jailed.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Quantifies the loss history that defines the risk premium on custodial interop designs and justifies paying up for non-custodial architectures.
insights.quote: bridges with custody of enormous pools of assets became the highest-value attack surfaces in crypto
insights.locator: In practice, bridges with custody

insights.claim: Across every major bridge failure the pattern was identical — custodial design concentrating risk in a small multisig or permissioned validator set that applications could not inspect, configure, or replace — so a single key leak, contract bug, or collusion took down the bridge and every application on it.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Reframes bridge hacks as a design-class failure rather than bad luck, making 'can the app configure and inspect its own verifiers?' the key diligence question for any interop exposure.
insights.quote: Across every major failure, the pattern was the same—custodial design that concentrated the risk.
insights.locator: Across every major failure

insights.claim: Canonical L2 bridges were structurally limited because each was chain-specific with no direct L2-to-L2 path, forcing every transaction back through Ethereum, and optimistic rollups' seven-day withdrawal window made time-sensitive capital allocation impossible while each bridge minted its own incompatible wrapped token.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The seven-day exit and wrapper incompatibility are the concrete mechanisms that made rollup liquidity non-fungible — the friction any credible interop or consolidation thesis has to remove.
insights.locator: The limitations to this strategy were structural.

insights.claim: Third-party bridges cut cross-chain settlement from seven days to minutes by connecting chains directly, but preserved the lock-mint-burn model behind a permissioned validator set — Wormhole's 19-node Guardian network, Multichain's distributed key generation — trading latency risk for custody risk.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Shows each interop generation solved speed while inheriting custody — the specific tradeoff the messaging model claims to break, and the test to apply to any bridge competitor.
insights.locator: In answer to canonical bridges that were too slow

insights.claim: The industry's first answer to fragmentation — sell on one chain and buy on another — is analogous to moving Coinbase stock from Schwab to Robinhood, where the in-kind ACATS transfer takes about a week so most investors instead eat taxes and the spread.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A TradFi analogy that makes the cost of missing in-kind transfer legible: the tax-and-spread drag is the value pool that native omnichain transfer captures.
insights.locator: The industry's first answer was to sell on one chain

insights.claim: LayerZero's core design choice was to move verified messages rather than assets, which shrinks the attack surface and removes the pooled-asset honeypot from the protocol layer by pushing liquidity ownership down to the applications themselves.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The structural reason a messaging protocol can scale value transferred without scaling the size of the target — the key differentiator versus liquidity-holding bridge competitors.
insights.quote: It is not a bridge. Bridges hold liquidity and execute swaps. LayerZero moves messages.
insights.locator: To clarify what LayerZero is not:

insights.claim: Decentralized Verifier Networks invert the prior security model by letting each application pick its own verifier set instead of the protocol dictating one, with Ondo, Paxos, and USDT0 all running their own DVNs to secure their token movements.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Application-configurable security is the feature that lets regulated issuers control their own trust assumptions — the wedge for institutional adoption that shared-security systems cannot offer.
insights.locator: DVNs invert the security model

insights.claim: In systems like Wormhole and Chainlink CCIP applications share one security model, so compromising the verification layer damages everything built on top — whereas per-application verifier configuration isolates that blast radius.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A direct competitive attack on the two largest rival messaging layers: correlated-failure risk is the criterion on which ARK expects institutional flows to choose.
insights.quote: In systems like Wormhole and Chainlink CCIP, applications share a security model which means that the compromise of their verification layers impacts everything built upon them.
insights.locator: Differentiated from other systems

insights.claim: Security is split into intrinsic guarantees hard-coded into immutable Endpoint contracts that not even LayerZero Labs can change, and extrinsic guarantees each application tunes — how many DVNs must sign, who runs them, what thresholds apply — as its value-at-risk grows.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Separates protocol risk from configuration risk, meaning due diligence on any omnichain asset must examine the app's own verifier settings, not just the protocol's reputation.
insights.locator: Two independent layers of security govern

insights.claim: In April 2026 an rsETH deployment running a 1-of-1 DVN configuration mismatched to its value-at-risk was exploited via a malicious message releasing tokens that should not have been released, but no other messages were forged and the remedy was a configuration change rather than a redesign.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The first live stress test of configurable security: the containment (one app, no protocol redesign) is the evidence ARK uses to argue the architecture held, and the benchmark against which any future incident should be judged.
insights.quote: The exploit was not a failure of the messaging primitive but a failure to adhere to the configuration required.
insights.locator: In April 2026, rsETH tested the protocol at scale.

insights.claim: ARK concedes LayerZero should have mandated multi-verifier setups from the start, and reports that after rsETH the protocol pushes a 3-of-3 DVN minimum default while LayerZero Labs now refuses to interact with 1/1 DVN setups.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A rare admission of design fault in a sponsored piece; watch whether 3-of-3 becomes enforced rather than encouraged, since permissionless defaults remain the residual risk.
insights.quote: a standard the protocol should have mandated from the beginning
insights.locator: LayerZero’s response has been to encourage applications

insights.claim: The subtler rsETH lesson is correlated exposure: when many applications converge on the same default verifier, configuration-level isolation matters far more than it appears, so defaults must be set as if every application were a $100+ million target.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Default settings, not the security ceiling, determine real systemic risk in permissionless infrastructure — a monitoring rule that generalizes well beyond crypto messaging.
insights.quote: defaults must be set as if every application were a $100+ million target. And now, each is.
insights.locator: rsETH also surfaced a subtler lesson

themes.theme: OFT Standard And The Stargate Reacquisition

insights.claim: Omnichain Fungible Token gives a token a single unified supply across chains via burn-and-mint at the token contract level, with no wrapped intermediary and no liquidity pool in between, while an OFT Adapter extends the same standard to tokens that cannot be modified by locking originals on their home chain.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Unified supply eliminates the wrapper discount and fragmented order books — the mechanism by which omnichain issuance should deepen liquidity for any token that adopts it.
insights.locator: The Killer Products: OFT & Stargate

insights.claim: More than 100 protocols have built on OFT powering roughly 600 token deployments, and OFT's share of volume across cross-chain token standards has fluctuated between 80% and 90% since 2024.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: An 80-90% standard share sustained over two years is the strongest evidence of a durable moat in the piece — track this ratio as the single best leading indicator of LayerZero's competitive position.
insights.locator: OFT—both with and without lzCompose—is becoming the industry standard

insights.claim: Stargate is positioned as the liquidity venue for non-OFT tokens, holding assets in transparent on-chain contracts at the application layer secured by LayerZero messaging rather than in a permissioned validator set holding keys.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Defines a division of labor — protocol moves messages, apps own liquidity — that lets the same stack serve both natively omnichain assets and legacy tokens.
insights.locator: OFT and Stargate serve different needs

insights.claim: LayerZero incubated Stargate, spun it out as a DAO in 2022, then reacquired it in 2025 for roughly $110 million in an all-token deal approved by 95% of voting token holders, who chose it over a higher all-cash counterbid from Wormhole.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: A rare data point on DAO governance preferring ecosystem alignment over price — and a signal that vertical integration of the flagship app is the setup for LayerZero's institutional push.
insights.quote: Choosing the incumbent's lower-priced offer spoke volumes about ecosystem alignment.
insights.locator: In 2025, LayerZero acquired Stargate from the DAO

insights.claim: As of June 2026 LayerZero reported $280 billion in cumulative value transferred, 44% of first-half 2026 cross-chain volume versus 41% for Circle's CCTP, $15+ billion processed through Stargate in 2025, roughly $100 billion of transfers via USDT0 as the largest OFT Adapter deployment, over 1 million messages a month across 66,000+ deployed contracts, and 170+ supported chains.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The full scorecard for the incumbency claim — note the 44% vs 41% gap over Circle's CCTP is narrow, so share leadership is contestable rather than settled.
insights.locator: As of June 2026, several statistics

insights.claim: Institutional DVN operators on the protocol already include Google Cloud, Fidelity's Center for Applied Technology, Worldpay, and Deutsche Telekom, alongside issuers such as Tether, Ethena, and PayPal's PYUSD issued by Paxos.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Named regulated operators running verification infrastructure is the clearest evidence that omnichain messaging is crossing into institutional production — watch for more payment and custody incumbents joining as DVNs.
insights.locator: Several institutional DVN operators

insights.claim: In the third-party bridge flow the collateral a lending protocol holds is a wrapped IOU of a fund token whose value depends on the bridge's solvency, and the manager earns the collateral's yield only if the wrapper passes it along — which most do not.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Yield leakage and bridge-solvency dependence are the specific reasons wrapped tokenized RWAs cannot serve as institutional collateral — the gap native omnichain issuance closes.
insights.locator: Third-Party Bridge.

insights.claim: With lzCompose, a manager holding a tokenized money market fund on Ethereum can sign once and have the burn, mint, collateral deposit, and SOL borrow execute as a single composed message flow, never sitting unhedged in an unproductive intermediate state as a non-composable transfer would require.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Composability collapses cross-chain execution risk into one signature — the concrete workflow that would let treasury desks use tokenized funds as live cross-chain collateral.
insights.quote: The manager goes from idle fund shares on Ethereum to a levered Solana-native position in one signature
insights.locator: Composable OFT (lzCompose).

insights.claim: The worked institutional example is a $20 million position in a NAV-stable, Treasury-backed tokenized money market fund on Ethereum earning 4.8% annually, posted as collateral on a Solana lending protocol to borrow SOL for a higher-yielding strategy without redeeming the underlying.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Names the target use case for omnichain rails — cross-chain collateral mobility for tokenized Treasuries — which is where RWA growth and interop demand intersect.
insights.locator: Consider a simple, hypothetical institutional example.

themes.theme: Chain-Premium Collapse And The Zero Pivot

insights.claim: The premium once paid for launching a chain has collapsed under a flood of L2 and app-chain tokens, so investors no longer pay high multiples for similar applications wrapped in new tickers.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: If the chain-launch premium is gone, new L2/app-chain token issuance should slow and existing ones face multiple compression — an explicit short-side implication of the consolidation thesis.
insights.quote: Investors no longer pay high multiples for similar applications wrapped in new tickers.
insights.locator: The premium associated with launching a chain has collapsed

insights.claim: The same financial incentives that once pushed teams toward fragmentation are now forcing consolidation, leaving only two engineering problems — throughput and support for specialized applications — standing between the market and a re-unified base layer.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The central directional call of the piece: bet on chain consolidation rather than continued proliferation, and on whoever solves throughput plus specialization at the base layer.
insights.quote: The financial incentives that once pushed teams toward fragmentation now are forcing consolidation.
insights.locator: The financial incentives that once pushed teams

insights.claim: After integrating 170+ chains, the team concluded that interoperability alone is not enough because messaging can connect fragmented networks but cannot emulate all environments to deliver shared liquidity and synchronous composability in one state.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The market leader in interop publicly capping its own category is the strategic tell behind the pivot to building a base layer — and a warning that pure messaging value accrual may plateau.
insights.quote: Messaging can connect fragmented networks but cannot emulate all environments to offer shared liquidity and synchronous composability in one state.
insights.locator: a vantage point that caused an uncomfortable conclusion

insights.claim: Deploying an Endpoint required rewriting it from scratch for each chain's bytecode, opcodes, consensus quirks, finality model, and gas semantics across EVM, MoveVM, SVM, Cosmos chains, and Bitcoin sidechains, with surface-level similarities hiding deep architectural differences — MoveVM's lack of native EVM-style contract interactions is what forced the invention of lzCompose.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The integration work is the moat: 170+ bespoke low-level rewrites are hard to replicate quickly and are the accumulated knowledge base ARK says underwrites the new L1.
insights.locator: Results Of LayerZero’s Integration Work

insights.claim: The team's conviction is that rebuilding every layer of the stack from first principles would compound improvements into performance gains orders of magnitude beyond any single breakthrough, which is the stated motivation for a new Layer 1 called Zero to be detailed in Part 2.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: Sets up the actual investable event — a new L1 launch from an incumbent interop team — and the specific claim (compounding, orders-of-magnitude gains) that Part 2 must substantiate.
insights.locator: After five years of detailed and complicated work

insights.claim: ARK Investment Management discloses that it and its affiliates are investors in LayerZero Labs and the ZRO token, have entered into material agreements with LayerZero Labs, and have an incentive to promote both, while noting the article reflects an inherent bias toward positive expected results.
insights.speaker: ARK Invest Research
insights.so_what: The piece is sponsored-adjacent research from a holder of the token it analyzes — discount the competitive claims about Wormhole and CCIP accordingly and verify share data independently.
insights.quote: have an incentive to promote LayerZero Labs and the ZRO Token
